guide.title: Cellular energetics: review guide
guide.intro: Cells capture, store, and use energy. This unit explains how enzymes speed reactions, how ATP couples energy-releasing and energy-using reactions, and how photosynthesis and cellular respiration transform energy.

sections.title: Enzymes
body: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins. Each has an active site whose shape and charge fit a specific substrate. Enzymes speed reactions by lowering the activation energy; they aren't used up and don't change ΔG.

Temperature, pH, and inhibitors affect enzymes. Above the optimum temperature, or far from the optimum pH, an enzyme can denature (lose its shape) and stop working. A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and can be outcompeted by adding more substrate; a noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere, changes the enzyme's shape, and lowers the maximum rate even at high substrate concentrations.
points: Rate rises with substrate concentration until all active sites are busy.
Cold slows enzymes without denaturing them.

sections.title: Cellular energy
body: Living systems need a constant input of energy to stay organized, because every energy transformation releases some energy as heat and increases the entropy of the surroundings.

ATP hydrolysis (ATP → ADP + Pᵢ) releases energy. Cells couple it to energy-requiring (endergonic) reactions so the combined process is favorable, often by transferring a phosphate group to a reactant. Metabolic pathways are sequences of enzyme-catalyzed steps, often regulated by feedback.
points: Exergonic reactions release free energy; endergonic reactions require it.
Coupled reactions are favorable if their combined ΔG is negative.
Organisms lose order and die without a continual energy supply.

sections.title: Photosynthesis
body: In the light-dependent reactions (thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast), chlorophyll absorbs light, water is split (releasing O₂), and an electron transport chain pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space. H⁺ flowing back to the stroma through ATP synthase makes ATP, and electrons reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH.
The Calvin cycle (stroma) uses that ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂ into sugar. Overall: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
points: The O₂ released comes from water, not from CO₂.
The Calvin cycle doesn't use light directly, but it depends on the light reactions' products.

sections.title: Cellular respiration
body: Glycolysis (cytosol) splits glucose into two pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid (Krebs) cycle release CO₂ and make NADH and FADH₂.

In the electron transport chain (inner mitochondrial membrane), electrons from NADH and FADH₂ pass along proteins that pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space; O₂ is the final electron acceptor, forming water. H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase makes most of the ATP (chemiosmosis). Without O₂, fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.
points: Most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation, not glycolysis.
Fermentation makes no extra ATP beyond glycolysis.
An uncoupler makes the inner membrane leaky to H⁺, so energy is released as heat instead of making ATP.

example.prompt: A reaction with ΔG = +20 kJ/mol is coupled to ATP hydrolysis (ΔG = −30 kJ/mol). Is the coupled process favorable?
example.solution: Add the free energy changes: +20 + (−30) = −10 kJ/mol. The total is negative, so the coupled process is favorable.

misconceptions: They are regenerated and can be used again.
The O₂ comes from splitting water.
“Plants photosynthesize instead of doing cellular respiration.”
Plants do both; their mitochondria carry out respiration.
“Glycolysis makes most of a cell's ATP.”
Most ATP comes from the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis.

questions.prompt: How does an enzyme speed up a reaction?
choices: It is consumed as a reactant
It raises the temperature of the cell
It lowers the activation energy
It makes ΔG more negative
questions.explanation: An enzyme provides a pathway with a lower energy barrier, so more molecules can react.
choiceExplanations: Enzymes are regenerated, not consumed.
Enzymes don't heat the cell.
Enzymes don't change the free energy difference between reactants and products.

questions.prompt: Why does each enzyme usually act on only one substrate or a few similar ones?
choices: It works only at one temperature
It is made of DNA that matches the substrate
Its active site's shape and charge fit only certain substrates
It contains the substrate's genes
questions.explanation: The active site is complementary to its substrate, which makes enzymes specific.
choiceExplanations: Enzymes work over a range of temperatures.
Most enzymes are proteins, not DNA.
Enzymes don't contain genes.

questions.prompt: An enzyme's reaction rate drops sharply when the temperature rises well above its optimum. What is the best explanation?
choices: The activation energy of the reaction increases
The enzyme denatures: its shape, including the active site, changes
The substrate molecules move too slowly
The enzyme makes more product than the cell needs
questions.explanation: High temperatures disrupt the bonds that hold the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.
choiceExplanations: The barrier doesn't rise; the enzyme stops working.
Molecules move faster at higher temperatures.
Product amount doesn't explain a sharp drop in rate.

questions.prompt: A competitive inhibitor slows an enzyme. How can its effect be overcome?
choices: It can't be overcome
By adding more inhibitor
By lowering the temperature
By adding much more substrate
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site, so with enough substrate the substrate wins most of the time.
choiceExplanations: Competitive inhibition is overcome by high substrate concentrations.
More inhibitor slows the enzyme further.
Lower temperature slows all enzyme reactions.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: With inhibitor X present, an enzyme's maximum reaction rate stays lower than normal even at very high substrate concentrations. How does X most likely act?
choices: It acts as a second substrate
It binds the active site and competes with the substrate
It binds a site other than the active site and changes the enzyme's shape (noncompetitive or allosteric inhibition)
It increases the activation energy of the uncatalyzed reaction
questions.explanation: Extra substrate can't displace an inhibitor bound elsewhere, so the maximum rate stays lower.
choiceExplanations: A second substrate would be used up, not lower the maximum rate.
A competitive inhibitor's effect would disappear at high substrate concentrations.
The uncatalyzed reaction's barrier isn't what changes.

questions.prompt: How do cells use ATP to power energy-requiring processes?
choices: It absorbs heat from the surroundings
Its hydrolysis to ADP and phosphate releases energy that is coupled to those processes
Breaking it down uses up energy
It is a long-term energy store like fat
questions.explanation: ATP hydrolysis is exergonic; coupling it to an endergonic process makes the combination favorable.
choiceExplanations: ATP releases energy; it doesn't absorb heat to do work.
Hydrolyzing ATP releases energy.
ATP is short-term currency; fats store energy long-term.

questions.prompt: A reaction with ΔG = +20 kJ/mol is coupled to ATP hydrolysis (ΔG = −30 kJ/mol). What is the ΔG of the coupled process?
choices: −50 kJ/mol, so it is favorable
−10 kJ/mol, so it is favorable
+50 kJ/mol, so it is unfavorable
+10 kJ/mol, so it is unfavorable
questions.explanation: Coupled free energy changes add: +20 + (−30) = −10 kJ/mol.
choiceExplanations: This adds the sizes as if both were negative.
This subtracts the negative value.
This has the wrong sign.

questions.prompt: Why must living cells take in energy continually?
choices: Energy is destroyed in chemical reactions
Only dividing cells need energy
Cells store unlimited energy and must keep filling it
Every energy transformation releases some energy as heat, so keeping cells organized requires a constant input
questions.explanation: Energy isn't destroyed, but it is lost as heat, and maintaining order requires replacing it.
choiceExplanations: Energy is conserved; it changes form, often to heat.
All living cells need energy to stay organized.
Cells can't store unlimited energy.

questions.prompt: In a pathway A → B → C → D, the end product D binds to and inhibits the first enzyme. What does this accomplish?
choices: It turns D back into A
It makes the first enzyme a substrate
It slows the pathway when enough D is present, conserving resources (feedback inhibition)
It speeds the pathway when D accumulates
questions.explanation: End-product inhibition is negative feedback: production slows when D is plentiful and resumes when D is used up.
choiceExplanations: Inhibition doesn't reverse the reactions.
D regulates the enzyme; the enzyme isn't consumed.
Inhibiting the first enzyme slows the pathway.

questions.prompt: Where do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place, and what do they produce?
choices: In the thylakoid membranes; they produce ATP, NADPH, and O₂
In the stroma; they produce glucose
In the mitochondria; they produce CO₂
In the cytosol; they produce pyruvate
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll and the electron transport chain are in the thylakoid membranes, where water is split and ATP and NADPH are made.
choiceExplanations: Sugar is made in the Calvin cycle in the stroma.
Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration.
Pyruvate is made in glycolysis.

questions.prompt: A plant is given water made with a heavy isotope of oxygen (¹⁸O); its CO₂ has ordinary oxygen. Where does the heavy oxygen first appear?
choices: In the O₂ the plant releases
In the glucose the plant makes
It stays in the water
In the CO₂ the plant takes in
questions.explanation: Splitting water in the light reactions releases its oxygen as O₂.
choiceExplanations: Glucose's oxygen comes from CO₂ in the Calvin cycle.
The water is split, so its oxygen leaves as O₂.
The plant takes in CO₂ from the air, which isn't labeled.

questions.prompt: What does the Calvin cycle use, and what does it make?
choices: It uses light and water to make O₂
It uses sugar to make CO₂
It uses glucose and O₂ to make ATP
It uses ATP, NADPH, and CO₂ to make sugar
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ into sugar using the energy and electrons from the light reactions.
choiceExplanations: That describes the light-dependent reactions.
That describes respiration's release of CO₂.
That describes cellular respiration.

questions.prompt: In a chloroplast, ATP synthase makes ATP as H⁺ ions flow in which direction?
choices: From the stroma into the thylakoid space
From the thylakoid space into the stroma
Out of the chloroplast
From the cytosol into the chloroplast
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space; H⁺ flows back down its gradient to the stroma through ATP synthase.
choiceExplanations: That is the direction H⁺ is pumped, against its gradient.
The gradient is inside the chloroplast.
The H⁺ gradient is across the thylakoid membrane, not the outer membranes.

questions.prompt: Where does glycolysis take place, and what is its net ATP yield per glucose?
choices: In the mitochondrial matrix; 2 ATP
In the inner mitochondrial membrane; 4 ATP
In the cytosol; about 30 ATP
In the cytosol; 2 ATP
questions.explanation: Glycolysis happens in the cytosol and nets 2 ATP (4 made, 2 used).
choiceExplanations: The citric acid cycle is in the matrix.
Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but uses 2, and it isn't in the membrane.
About 30 ATP is the total yield of aerobic respiration.

questions.prompt: What is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration?
choices: Oxygen, which forms water
NAD⁺
Glucose
CO₂
questions.explanation: O₂ accepts electrons and H⁺ at the end of the chain, forming H₂O.
choiceExplanations: NAD⁺ accepts electrons earlier, becoming NADH.
Glucose is the fuel, not the final acceptor.
CO₂ is released in the citric acid cycle.

questions.prompt: Without oxygen, yeast carry out fermentation. What is the main purpose of fermentation?
choices: To make much more ATP than aerobic respiration
To regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep making ATP
To make oxygen
To build glucose from CO₂
questions.explanation: Glycolysis needs NAD⁺. Fermentation passes NADH's electrons to pyruvate (or a product of it), freeing NAD⁺.
choiceExplanations: Fermentation adds no ATP beyond glycolysis's 2.
Fermentation doesn't produce O₂.
Building sugar from CO₂ is photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to H⁺. What happens?
choices: Electron transport and O₂ use continue, but ATP production falls and more energy is released as heat
Electron transport stops immediately
ATP production rises because H⁺ moves faster
Glycolysis stops because it needs the H⁺ gradient
questions.explanation: H⁺ leaks back without passing through ATP synthase, so the gradient's energy becomes heat instead of ATP.
choiceExplanations: The chain can keep running, since the gradient no longer builds up to resist it.
ATP synthase makes ATP only when H⁺ flows through it.
Glycolysis doesn't depend on the mitochondrial H⁺ gradient.

questions.prompt: Where does the citric acid (Krebs) cycle take place?
choices: In the mitochondrial matrix
In the nucleus
In the cytosol
In the thylakoid membranes
questions.explanation: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and is oxidized in the matrix, where the citric acid cycle releases CO₂.
choiceExplanations: The nucleus holds DNA.
Glycolysis is in the cytosol.
Thylakoids are in chloroplasts.
